questions.question: What does Part 2 of the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus say if $F$ is an antiderivative of $f$ on $[a,b]$?
How does Part 2 of the Fundamental Theorem let you evaluate a definite integral?
options: By ignoring both the lower and upper integration bounds
By using only the midpoint value of the interval
Only through a numerical approximation of the area
By evaluating an antiderivative at both integration bounds

questions.question: Use Part 2 to evaluate $\int_0^1 x^2\,\mathrm{d}x$.
Use Part 2 to evaluate $\int_a^b 1\,\mathrm{d}x$.
What does Part 2 of the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus use from an antiderivative?
options: The value of the definite integral depends on every intermediate derivative of an antiderivative.
A definite integral can be evaluated only when the integrand is constant.
The lower and upper bounds play no role in the value of the integral.
The value of the definite integral depends only on the boundary values of an antiderivative.

questions.question: What information do you need in order to apply Part 2 directly to $\int_a^b f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x$?
options: Only the derivative $F'$ of an antiderivative.
The value of $f$ at the midpoint $\dfrac{a+b}{2}$ only.
An antiderivative $F$ of $f$ and the values of $F$ at $a$ and $b$.

questions.question: Let $F(x) = x^3-x$ be an antiderivative of $f$ on $[0,2]$. What is $\int_0^2 f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x$?
Suppose $F$ is an antiderivative of $f$ and $F(1) = 3$, $F(5) = 11$. What is $\int_1^5 f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x$?
If $F$ is an antiderivative of $f$, which change to $F$ leaves the value of $F(b)-F(a)$ unchanged?
options: Replacing $F$ by $F^2$, which changes endpoint values nonlinearly.

questions.question: Which assumption from the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus (Part 2) is essential before writing $\int_a^b f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x = F(b)-F(a)$?
options: $F$ must be an antiderivative of $f$ on $[a,b]$.

questions.question: Suppose $F$ is an antiderivative of $f$ on $[a,b]$, and define $G(x) = F(x)+7$. What is $G(b)-G(a)$?
Let $F$ be an antiderivative of $f$ with $F(a) = m$ and $F(b) = n$. Using Part 2, what is $\int_a^b f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x$?
What role does an antiderivative play in Part 2 of the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus?
options: It replaces the endpoints by infinity, no matter which values are selected.
It gives only the midpoint value.
It is evaluated at the endpoints to compute the definite integral.
It proves that the integrand is zero.

questions.question: If $F$ is an antiderivative of $f$, which relation holds?
What does $F(x)\big|_{x=a}^{b}$ mean in Part 2?
Evaluate $\int_0^2 x\,\mathrm{d}x$ using Part 2.
If $F$ is an antiderivative of $f$, $F(0)=1$, and $F(3)=10$, what is $\int_0^3 f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x$?
Evaluate $\int_2^5 1\,\mathrm{d}x$.
Why does adding a constant to an antiderivative not change the value from Part 2?
Use $F(x)=x^4/4$ to evaluate $\int_1^2 x^3\,\mathrm{d}x$.
